extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent prosecutors, and applicants handling nature-based product claims (Section 101 issues)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether composition/product claims involving natural products (mixtures, carriers, dosages, casings) are directed to a natural product under 35 U.S.C. §101, following MPEP 2106 (Sections 2A & 2B) and recent Federal Circuit/Board practice (e.g., In re Bhagat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 2A: Is the claim directed to a product of nature?
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2A requires the Examiner to analyze whether or not the claim is directed to a natural product. If there is more than one claim element that could be a natural product, they are to be evaluated to see if they occur together in nature. If they do not, the components are each compared to their closest naturally occurring counterpart to see if any of the components is clearly not a product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each potentially nature-based claim element independently and in combination; determine whether the claimed combination or each component as claimed has a counterpart in nature. Use factual comparisons to closest natural counterparts; do not shortcut by conflating with anticipation/obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics requirement (2A analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: If none of the claim elements is clearly not a product of nature, the nature-based combination is examined to see if the combination of components has 'markedly different' characteristics due to the interactions in the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked difference typically requires evidence of some change in physical or chemical properties (for a single nature-based product) or evidence of interaction between multiple natural products. Examples: changes in oxidative stability when ratios change; functional/structural changes attributable to formulation or delivery form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carriers/non-natural components can render claim patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Carriers for a natural product that is the active ingredient, which are not themselves natural products (e.g., nanoparticles), will often have structural and physical characteristics that distinguish them from their closest natural counterparts and therefore can render a claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether claimed carriers or excipients possess structural/physical properties not found in nature. If so, the inquiry under 2A can end in favor of eligibility. Cite Examples 3 and 4 of the Interim Examination Guidelines as support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed to Step 2B only if claim is no more than a natural product or simple combination lacking marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim encompasses no more than a natural product or a simple combination thereof, and the marked difference is absent, the Examiner will subject the claim to the Step 2B analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure Step 2A is fully resolved before moving to 2B. Don’t assume Step 2B until the marked-difference assessment is documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B "inventive concept" standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Step 2B the claim must possess a further 'inventive concept' that renders it 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (the nature-based product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO Guidelines say inventive-concept questions should not be decided on the basis of §§102/103 analysis, but in practice courts/boards often rely on prior-art style reasoning. Be prepared to show functional/structural features that add significantly more than mere natural phenomena or routine activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate §101 analysis with §102/§103 anticipation/obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis under section 101 is separate from patentability analysis under sections 102 or 103, and examiners/courts should not simply carry over rationale from anticipation/obviousness into the §101 inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using specification statements that elements are 'not limiting' (a §102/103 style rationale) to defeat §101 eligibility. Step 2A and 2B require their own factual showings (e.g., marked difference, inventive concept) rather than simple citation that a reference discloses components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain-words claim construction in §101 context
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be examined by the plain words of the claims in context of surrounding words (e.g., 'contained in one or more complementing casings providing controlled delivery of the formulation to a subject' should be treated as recited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not collapse or paraphrase a detailed claim limitation into a generic term (e.g., reducing the quoted casing language to 'casing') when assessing whether a limitation is a non-natural element or imparts structure/function for §101 purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's burden to present evidence of marked difference or non-nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must provide adequate evidence (e.g., scientific publications, PHOSITA testimony, experimental data) that the claimed compositions/mixtures/dosages/casings are not found in nature or are markedly different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document empirical studies, expert declarations, and publications showing how manipulation (storing, extracting, mixing, encasing) changes composition/properties (e.g., oxidative stability changes with ratio shifts) and that claimed ratios/concentrations/configurations do not occur in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires same part-to-part relationship; 'intermixtures' must be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation law requires the same part-to-part relationship; references that do not disclose the claimed intermixtures or specific ratios do not anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing against an anticipation rejection, show that prior art does not disclose the claimed combination or the particular quantitative ranges/ratios and that the references fail to disclose intermixtures in the claimed manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dosage and controlled-delivery limitations can be non-natural, functional/structural additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations reciting 'dosage' and 'casings providing controlled delivery' may not exist in nature and can change characteristics of natural products (e.g., avoid concentrated delivery of specific phytochemicals that may be harmful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence showing natural products lack predictable dosages or controlled delivery (e.g., lipid profiles in natural sources are variable) to support that claimed dosage/delivery limitations add 'significantly more' or at least satisfy 2A marked-difference analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed specific ratios/concentrations support non-nature and patentability if not found in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting specific ratios of polyunsaturated, monounsaturated, and saturated fatty acids (or specific omega-6/omega-3 ranges) that are NOT known in nature can distinguish the claims from natural products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out examiner failures when no prior product or oil is cited that meets the claimed ratios; provide comparative compositional data to show claimed ranges are novel relative to natural sources such as olive or walnut oil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of Board/court practice of importing anticipation findings into §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board and courts often apply anticipation-style reasoning to §101 (e.g., holding that elements are 'not limiting' per the specification and therefore do not provide patentability), effectively conflating §102/103 with §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prosecuting appeals or petitions, object to mixing analyses and insist on separate §101 factual findings (2A/2B). Emphasize distinct legal standards from Mayo and the MPEP and show why prior-art conclusions should not be determinative of §101 eligibility.
